label: UDFs & Stored Procedures — Overview & Privileges
topic: Snowflake UDFs and Stored Procedures — Variations, Handler Languages, Access Control, Calling Conventions

questions.stem: What does a scalar user-defined function (UDF) return?

options.text: One output row with a single column/value for each input row
A tabular result set with multiple columns and rows
A status message indicating success or failure
Multiple rows grouped by an aggregation key

explanation.correct: A scalar UDF returns one output row for each input row. The returned row consists of a single column/value.

distractors.B: Tabular results with multiple columns and rows are returned by a UDTF, not a scalar UDF.
distractors.C: UDFs return explicit values from expressions, not status messages.
distractors.D: Aggregation across multiple rows is performed by a UDAF, not a scalar UDF.

questions.stem: Which TWO handler languages produce UDFs that are sharable with Snowflake Secure Data Sharing?

options.text: Java and Python
Python and Scala
Java and JavaScript
JavaScript and SQL

explanation.correct: Only JavaScript and SQL handlers produce UDFs that are sharable with Secure Data Sharing. Java, Python, and Scala UDFs have limitations on sharing.

distractors.A: Java and Python UDFs have documented limitations that prevent sharing.
distractors.B: Neither Python nor Scala UDFs are sharable.
distractors.C: Java UDFs have sharing limitations; only JavaScript UDFs are sharable among non-SQL languages.

questions.stem: What privilege is required on a schema to create a stored procedure?

options.text: CREATE TABLE
CREATE PROCEDURE
OWNERSHIP on the database
ACCOUNTADMIN role

explanation.correct: Creating a stored procedure requires the CREATE PROCEDURE privilege on the schema, along with USAGE on the database and schema.

distractors.A: CREATE TABLE is for table creation, not stored procedures.
distractors.C: OWNERSHIP on the database is far more privileged than needed.
distractors.D: ACCOUNTADMIN is not required; any role with CREATE PROCEDURE can create procedures.

questions.stem: Which THREE UDF variations are available in Snowflake? (Select THREE)

options.text: User-defined index function (UDIF)
User-defined aggregate function (UDAF)
User-defined trigger function (UDTRF)
User-defined table function (UDTF)
Vectorized user-defined function
User-defined constraint function (UDCF)

explanation.correct: Snowflake supports UDAFs (aggregate across rows), UDTFs (return tabular values), and vectorized UDFs (receive Pandas DataFrames for batch processing), in addition to scalar UDFs.

distractors.A: There is no user-defined index function concept in Snowflake.
distractors.C: Snowflake does not support triggers or user-defined trigger functions.
distractors.F: There is no user-defined constraint function in Snowflake.

questions.stem: Which TWO ways can you create a stored procedure without requiring CREATE PROCEDURE privilege? (Select TWO)

options.text: Create a stored procedure with EXECUTE AS CALLER
Create a stored procedure owned by the PUBLIC role
Create a temporary stored procedure using the TEMP or TEMPORARY parameter
Create an anonymous procedure using CALL (with anonymous procedure)
Create a stored procedure in the INFORMATION_SCHEMA

explanation.correct: Temporary procedures (TEMP/TEMPORARY) and anonymous procedures (CALL WITH) do not require the CREATE PROCEDURE privilege.

distractors.A: EXECUTE AS CALLER affects the rights execution model, not whether CREATE PROCEDURE privilege is needed.
distractors.B: Assigning ownership to PUBLIC does not bypass the privilege requirement.
distractors.E: Users cannot create stored procedures in INFORMATION_SCHEMA.

questions.stem: Which THREE privileges are required by a role to call a UDF? (Select THREE)

options.text: USAGE on the database containing the UDF
CREATE FUNCTION on the schema
USAGE on the schema containing the UDF
OWNERSHIP on the function
USAGE on the function itself
READ on the internal stage holding dependencies

explanation.correct: Calling a UDF requires USAGE on the database, USAGE on the schema, and USAGE on the function.

distractors.B: CREATE FUNCTION is needed for creation, not for calling an existing UDF.
distractors.D: OWNERSHIP is not required to call a function; USAGE on the function suffices.
distractors.F: Stage READ is needed only when the function depends on staged files, and is in addition to the core three.

questions.scenario: A developer writes a Python UDF that references CURRENT_DATABASE() within the handler code. The UDF is created in database ANALYTICS_DB but is called from a session where the active database is SALES_DB.
questions.stem: Which database name does CURRENT_DATABASE() return inside the handler?

options.text: ANALYTICS_DB — the database that contains the UDF
SALES_DB — the caller's active database
NULL — context functions are not available in UDF handlers
An error is raised because CURRENT_DATABASE() is not permitted in handlers

explanation.correct: If CURRENT_DATABASE or CURRENT_SCHEMA is specified in UDF handler code, the function returns the database or schema that contains the UDF, not the one in use for the session.

distractors.B: The caller's session context does not determine what CURRENT_DATABASE returns inside a UDF handler.
distractors.C: These context functions are available and return the UDF's own location.
distractors.D: No error is raised; the functions work but resolve to the UDF's containing database/schema.

questions.scenario: A team needs to call a stored procedure with three arguments, but only wants to provide the first and third, using the default for the second.
questions.stem: How should they call the procedure?

options.text: Pass NULL as the second argument in positional notation
Omit the second argument in positional notation and list only the first and third
Use named arguments, specifying only the first and third by name
Set a session variable for the second argument before calling

explanation.correct: When you need to omit an optional argument and specify a later one, you must use named arguments. Positional notation does not allow skipping middle arguments.

distractors.A: Passing NULL is not the same as using the default value; the parameter would receive NULL.
distractors.B: Positional notation requires arguments in order — you cannot skip a middle argument.
distractors.D: Session variables are not used to supply stored procedure argument defaults.

questions.scenario: A stored procedure failed halfway through its execution. The first three statements succeeded, but the fourth raised an error.
questions.stem: What is the state of the changes made by the first three statements?

options.text: All three are automatically rolled back because stored procedures are atomic
Only DDL statements from the first three are rolled back; DML remains
The outcome depends on whether the procedure runs with owner's or caller's rights
The first three statements remain committed because stored procedures are NOT atomic

explanation.correct: Stored procedures are not atomic. If one statement fails, the other statements are not necessarily rolled back.

distractors.A: Stored procedures are explicitly documented as not atomic.
distractors.B: There is no DDL-specific rollback behavior; all successful statements persist.
distractors.C: The rights model does not affect atomicity behavior.

questions.scenario: A developer wants to call a stored procedure and use its return value within a SELECT statement outside of a Snowflake Scripting block.
questions.stem: Is this possible?

options.text: Yes — CALL can be used as a subquery in any SELECT
No — outside a Snowflake Scripting block, the CALL return value cannot be part of an expression
Yes — by wrapping the CALL in a CTE
Yes — if the procedure is defined as a UDTF

explanation.correct: Outside of a Snowflake Scripting block, the value returned by a stored procedure cannot be used because the CALL cannot be part of an expression.

distractors.A: CALL statements cannot be embedded as subqueries in standard SQL SELECT statements.
distractors.C: CTEs do not support CALL statements as their source.
distractors.D: A UDTF is a function, not a stored procedure; stored procedures are called with CALL.

questions.scenario: A team wants to write a UDF with a Python handler and store the handler code on a stage rather than inline.
questions.stem: Is this supported?

options.text: No — Python handlers must always be inline
Only if the UDF is defined as a UDTF
Yes — Python supports both inline and staged handler locations
Only if the Python version is 3.8 or higher

explanation.correct: Python handlers support both inline and staged handler locations. Java and Scala also support staged handlers.

distractors.A: Python is one of the languages that supports staged handlers.
distractors.B: Both scalar UDFs and UDTFs with Python handlers can use staged code.
distractors.D: The handler location support is independent of the specific Python runtime version.

questions.scenario: Two stored procedures in the same schema have the same name but accept different argument types.
questions.stem: How does Snowflake resolve which procedure to execute?

options.text: The most recently created procedure is always chosen
An error is raised because duplicate procedure names are not allowed
The caller must specify the procedure's internal ID
Procedures are resolved by their argument types (overloading), and named arguments can further disambiguate

explanation.correct: Stored procedures are identified and resolved by both their name and argument types (overloading). Named arguments can further disambiguate if types overlap.

distractors.A: Creation order does not determine resolution.
distractors.B: Duplicate names with different signatures are explicitly allowed — this is overloading.
distractors.C: There is no internal ID-based calling mechanism.

questions.scenario: A UDF accesses staged files during query execution. During the query, another user modifies one of the referenced staged files.
questions.stem: What happens?

options.text: The UDF automatically uses the modified version of the file
The query continues with the original version of the file
The query is paused until the file modification completes
The function call fails with an error

explanation.correct: If staged files referenced in a query are modified or deleted while the query is running, the function call fails with an error.

distractors.A: The UDF does not automatically pick up modified files mid-query.
distractors.B: Snowflake does not snapshot staged files for the duration of the query.
distractors.C: There is no pause mechanism; the concurrent modification results in an error.

questions.scenario: A data engineer is evaluating which handler languages support ONLY inline handler code for UDFs.
questions.stem: Which TWO handler languages support ONLY inline handler code? (Select TWO)

options.text: Java
Python
JavaScript
SQL
Scala

explanation.correct: JavaScript and SQL handlers support inline handler code only. Java, Python, and Scala support both inline and staged.

distractors.A: Java supports both inline and staged handler locations.
distractors.B: Python supports both inline and staged handler locations.
distractors.E: Scala supports both inline and staged handler locations.

questions.scenario: A platform team is comparing UDFs and stored procedures to decide which to use for a new feature.
questions.stem: Which THREE characteristics differentiate stored procedures from UDFs? (Select THREE)

options.text: Stored procedures are always faster than UDFs
Stored procedures can execute with owner's rights, delegating privileged operations
Stored procedures return tabular results by default
Stored procedures can perform branching, looping, and other procedural constructs
Stored procedures are called with CALL statements and cannot be used in expressions
Stored procedures are always atomic

explanation.correct: Stored procedures can run with owner's rights, support procedural code, and are invoked with CALL (not usable in expressions outside Snowflake Scripting).

distractors.A: Performance depends on the workload; stored procedures are not inherently faster.
distractors.C: Stored procedures return a single value by default; tabular returns are supported only in specific handler languages.
distractors.F: Stored procedures are explicitly documented as NOT atomic.

questions.scenario: A team wants to automate a nightly cleanup task that deletes old data from multiple tables, where the cutoff date is passed as a parameter.
questions.stem: Which TWO advantages does a stored procedure provide for this use case? (Select TWO)

options.text: The procedure automatically retries failed statements
The procedure encapsulates multiple DELETE statements in a single callable object
The procedure prevents any data loss by creating automatic backups
The procedure can be granted to roles that lack direct DELETE privileges on the tables
The procedure runs without consuming warehouse credits

explanation.correct: An owner's rights stored procedure can delegate DELETE operations to roles without direct table privileges, and it encapsulates all cleanup logic in a single callable, reusable object.

distractors.A: Stored procedures do not automatically retry failed statements; they are not atomic.
distractors.C: Stored procedures do not create automatic backups; Time Travel handles data recovery.
distractors.E: Stored procedures use the caller's current warehouse and do consume credits.

questions.scenario: A governance team is documenting the privilege model for UDF ownership.
questions.stem: Which TWO privileges must the UDF owner role maintain after creation? (Select TWO)

options.text: CREATE FUNCTION on the schema
USAGE on the function for the owner
USAGE on the database containing the UDF
USAGE on the schema containing the UDF
SELECT on any tables the UDF references

explanation.correct: After a UDF is created, the owner must maintain USAGE on both the database and the schema, plus OWNERSHIP on the function itself.

distractors.A: CREATE FUNCTION is needed only at creation time, not for ongoing ownership.
distractors.B: The owner has OWNERSHIP which inherently includes USAGE; no separate USAGE grant is needed.
distractors.E: Required privileges depend on what the handler does, not a blanket SELECT requirement.

questions.scenario: A developer wants to store handler code on a stage for versioning. They need to know which handler languages for stored procedures support ONLY inline code.
questions.stem: Which TWO handler languages support ONLY inline code for stored procedures? (Select TWO)

options.text: Java
JavaScript
Python
Scala
Snowflake Scripting

explanation.correct: JavaScript and Snowflake Scripting handlers support inline code only for stored procedures. Java, Python, and Scala support both inline and staged.

distractors.A: Java supports both inline and staged handlers for stored procedures.
distractors.C: Python supports both inline and staged handlers for stored procedures.
distractors.D: Scala supports both inline and staged handlers for stored procedures.

questions.scenario: A Snowflake Scripting stored procedure creates a procedure-scoped temporary table inside its body to hold intermediate results.
questions.stem: When does this table get removed?

options.text: When the session ends
After the Time Travel retention period expires
When the procedure's execution completes — it is automatically removed
It must be explicitly dropped with a DROP TABLE statement inside the procedure

explanation.correct: A procedure-scoped temporary table exists only for the duration of a single execution of the procedure and is removed automatically when the procedure's scope ends.

distractors.A: Session-scoped temporary tables last for the session, but procedure-scoped ones are removed when the procedure completes.
distractors.B: Procedure-scoped tables do not enter Time Travel; they are discarded at procedure completion.
distractors.D: Procedure-scoped temporary tables are self-contained and removed automatically.

questions.scenario: A team calls a stored procedure specifying two arguments by name and one by position in the same CALL statement.
questions.stem: What is the result?

options.text: The call fails because you must specify ALL arguments either by name or by position, not both
The call succeeds because Snowflake can infer the position of the unnamed argument
Only the positional argument is used; the named arguments are ignored
The call succeeds if the positional argument is listed first

explanation.correct: You must either specify all arguments by name or by position. You cannot mix named and positional arguments in the same CALL statement.

distractors.B: Snowflake does not infer positions when mixing named and positional notation.
distractors.C: Snowflake does not silently ignore named arguments; mixed notation causes an error.
distractors.D: The order does not matter — mixing named and positional notation is always prohibited.
